analysis.one_liner: Phases out manufacturing and sale of toxic persistent chemicals like asbestos, lead, and mercury within five years.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors and never received a vote, dying in committee when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the EPA to identify and list "persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic" chemical substances — poisons that build up in people's bodies and the environment — and to phase out their manufacture, processing, and sale within five years. It named about twenty chemicals that would be restricted immediately, including asbestos, lead, mercury, and cadmium, while letting the EPA grant five-year exemptions for uses it found critical and essential, such as lead in car batteries or mercury in certain lamps. It died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor from either party.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially children, whose bodies are exposed to chemicals like lead, mercury, asbestos, and flame retardants that accumulate over time and are linked to developmental harm, cancer, and other diseases. Families living near chemical plants, landfills, or older housing would see the largest benefit, since these substances concentrate in soil, dust, and water. Some workers in safer substitutes and green chemistry would also gain as demand shifted away from the restricted chemicals.

how_it_helps.text: Required the EPA to phase out the manufacture, processing, and distribution of listed persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic chemicals within five years, with only narrow exemptions for critical or essential uses.

Named about twenty specific chemicals that would be restricted on the basis of existing scientific evidence, including asbestos, lead and lead compounds, mercury and mercury compounds, and cadmium, so protection would not have to wait for years of additional study.
Required the EPA to screen every new chemical submitted for review under the Toxic Substances Control Act to catch persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic substances before they entered commerce.
Required public disclosure of the EPA's determinations, the basis for them, and any conditions on manufacture or disposal, and let the public comment on industry petitions for exemptions.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and companies that make products containing the listed substances — such as makers of lead-acid batteries (which kept an exemption), electronics, flame retardants, and industrial materials — would bear compliance costs, reformulation expenses, and possible supply disruptions. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers in the prices of goods. Communities dependent on plants producing the listed chemicals could face job losses unless the industry shifted to substitutes.

drawbacks.text: A five-year phase-out of widely used industrial substances like lead, cadmium, and chlorinated paraffins could disrupt supply chains and raise costs for manufacturers and consumers, and some affected plants or jobs could be lost before substitutes are fully scaled up.

Listing specific chemicals directly in the bill, rather than letting the EPA's rulemaking process determine them, locks in a fixed list that only updates every three years and could miss newly identified hazards or overreach on borderline cases.

The exemption system, including presumptive allowances for lead-acid batteries and electronics uses exempted under the European Union's RoHS directive, leaves substantial continuing exposure to some of the same substances the bill targets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit is substantial: the listed chemicals are among the most studied toxins in commerce, and phasing them out would reduce exposure linked to childhood developmental harm, cancer, and environmental contamination that is extremely expensive to clean up. The costs — reformulation, compliance, and possible supply disruptions — are real but are the same costs the industry already faced under comparable European restrictions, and the bill's exemption process provided a pressure valve for genuinely essential uses. The design is aggressive but not reckless; the main weakness is that the bill got no refinement through hearings or committee work, so its rough edges were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2014, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and stayed there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on July 24, 2014, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No senator from either party cosponsored the bill, so its official cosponsor list was empty.
The committee took no further action: the full action history shows only the introduction and referral, and the bill never reached the Senate floor.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, without the bill receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and users of the listed chemicals — including producers of lead, mercury, cadmium, asbestos-containing products, and persistent flame retardants — are better off because the bill died, since they kept selling and using substances the bill would have phased out within five years.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Toxic chemical manufacturers kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-led agenda did not advance it to the floor.

against.name: Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: No Democratic senator signed on as a cosponsor despite a member of their caucus sponsoring the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a roll call, and its sponsorship pattern gives no partisan split to read: one Democrat introduced it and no senator of either party cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers (persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic substances)
industries.note: The bill would have forced companies making or selling listed chemicals — asbestos, mercury compounds, short-chain chlorinated paraffins, brominated flame retardants, and more — to phase them out within five years or win a narrow exemption. These substances profit by staying in commerce even though they accumulate in people's bodies and the environment, so the industry's interest ran directly against the public's.

industries.industry: Lead, mercury, and cadmium producers and industrial users
industries.note: Most uses would have been phased out, but the bill expressly presumed allowable some high-volume uses: lead in car batteries, and lead, cadmium, and mercury in electronics uses exempted under the EU's RoHS directive. Those users would have kept a regulated, continuing market rather than a full ban.
As toxic chemicals were phased out, makers of safer alternatives would have gained a market. Their interest lines up with the public's exposure reductions.
